place-work.text: A probable Constantinopolitan ivory image reveals carved form and an interpreted devotional use; separately excavated harbour timbers reveal fitting, sealing and repair. Together they explain kinds of urban work without identifying one workshop, transport route or universal household practice.

participation.text: Imperial and church institutions changed; Roman self-identification persisted across the modern label.

evidence.text: A tenth-century devotional object represents a particular practice, not every century of imperial life.

name: Byzantium: Romans across changing centuries
geographicPrecision: Capital locator on the Bosporus; no single imperial boundary.

interval.label: Conventional frame, 330–1453 CE
interval.note: New capital in 330 to Ottoman capture in 1453. Constantinople was under Latin rule 1204–1261; Byzantine states continued elsewhere. Not an uninterrupted single territorial unit.

question: Can political change and cultural continuity coexist?
summary: Carvers shaped portable ivory images while shipbuilders fitted and repaired wooden hulls in Constantinople’s harbour. A mid-tenth-century icon and separately excavated ship remains reveal concrete work within a changing Roman capital, without supplying one workshop, household or uninterrupted political story.

sections.title: Carving a portable image
sections.text: A carver shaped figures, columns and a pierced canopy in a small ivory panel. Removing material opened spaces through the frame; leaving material raised figures from the background. The surviving panel is 15.1 centimeters high. The Met attributes it probably to Constantinople and interprets it as a private devotional object, once completed by two folding wings. Those missing parts remind us that making an image also involved arranging how it could be opened, seen and closed. The photograph reveals the carving, while the catalogue supplies the material identification and proposed use.

sections.title: Fitting and maintaining a working hull
sections.text: At the Theodosian Harbour, ship remains reveal another kind of skilled work. The published study of the wreck called YK14 records fitted planks, wooden treenails and iron nails. Grass and pine pitch helped seal seams. Fitting parts together and sealing seams were different tasks in making a working hull. Repairs included reused pieces and renewed caulking: keeping a vessel working required attention after its first construction. These traces explain tasks through materials that survived in wet ground. They are a separately excavated urban context, not the ivory’s known journey. No cargo was recovered that could identify what this particular ship carried.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 53–55: YK14 construction and repairs

sections.title: Using and interpreting images
sections.text: Portable images joined material work to religious practice. Brooks describes icons made in several media and used in different settings; triptych wings could open and close around a central image. Their relationship to sacred subjects was debated. The selected ivory belongs after the reintroduction of images in 843, rather than to the capital’s foundation. Its Crucifixion scene invites attention to figures and inscriptions, but identifying every figure requires interpretation. Probable private devotion does not identify an original room, owner or the beliefs of every inhabitant.

citations.locator: Definition; Form and Function; Icons after Iconoclasm

sections.title: Keeping the wider history in view
sections.text: The people modern historians call Byzantine identified themselves as Romans. The case begins with Constantinople’s conventional dedication date in 330. Its capital story changes sharply in 1204, when crusaders took the city; Byzantine rule returned there in 1261. The case ends with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453; other Byzantine territories continued longer. Carving and hull repair illuminate bounded parts of that long history. A single timeline band cannot make them evidence for one unchanging territory, culture or form of government.

claims.text: The medieval inhabitants described themselves as Romans; Constantinople’s 1204–1261 Latin occupation interrupts a simple continuous-capital story.

deeperReading.title: Construction and deposition are different clocks
deeperReading.text: The YK14 report first discusses pottery-layer dating to the late ninth or early tenth century. Wood dating, including a timber likely associated with the ship, suggested construction in the first half of the ninth century. Repairs then belong between making and final deposition. The authors’ reasoning does not turn a dated piece of wood into a known launch day or make every component equally old. The reference marker around 900 locates a reported archaeological context. It does not redate construction to 843, establish an exact sinking year or reveal a cargo.

deeperReading.title: An inscription supports an argument
deeperReading.text: The reclining figure below the cross has been read as Hades or Adam. Margaret English Frazer argued for Hades by comparing the abbreviated inscription with other imagery and hymns. Her reading links the figure with an interpretation of Christ’s victory over death. It is an example of a scholar bringing several kinds of evidence together. The hymn passages remain mediated through her article: this reading supplies no new Greek translation, eyewitness ceremony or claim that every viewer understood the image alike.

deeperReading.title: A medium does not identify a workshop
deeperReading.text: Ryder places ivory images alongside secular caskets and discusses material supply and assembly. That context expands the kinds of work we can ask about. It does not locate this panel’s carver, identify its tusk or establish a particular workshop’s materials and labour arrangements.

evidenceReading.title: Carved surfaces, repaired timbers and an interpreted figure
evidenceReading.introduction: These passages are editorial paraphrases. Visible form, an excavation association and a scholarly argument answer different questions; no ship is identified as the ivory’s carrier.

items.label: A catalogue connects form with probable use
items.text: The Met identifies elephant ivory, a surviving central triptych panel and probable private devotional use, with production probably in Constantinople.
items.interpretation: The supplied photograph lets us examine openwork and relief. Material, date and probable use come from the catalogue. Missing wings and a likely setting do not establish a named household, patron or workshop; the photograph’s modern creation date is unknown.

items.label: Excavated repairs make maintenance visible
items.text: The YK14 report describes fitted and joined planks, caulking and repeated repairs, including reused pieces. Its construction estimate differs from pottery-layer dating.
items.interpretation: Material associations can explain work and successive changes. Wood age, original construction, repair and deposition must be distinguished. No recovered cargo connects the wreck to the selected ivory, and the selected report does not identify individual workers or wages.

items.label: An identification is tested by comparison
items.text: Frazer considers Hades and Adam as alternative readings of the reclining figure and uses an abbreviated inscription, other images and hymns to support Hades.
items.interpretation: The conclusion is an attributed comparative argument. It is more than naming a figure from its position, while remaining different from a new direct translation, universal agreement or proof of a particular performance.

familyActivity.title: What can an image show about work?
steps: Find an opening through the carved frame, a figure projecting from the background and a line of letters in the supplied photograph. Describe each before naming its meaning.

Ask an adult to read the capsule. Sort three statements: the frame has openings; the panel was probably used privately; a ship carried this exact ivory. Which is visible, which is a source interpretation, and which is not established?
Use the capsule to name two tasks recorded on the excavated ship. Explain why a repair can belong to a later stage than first construction.
Write one supported sentence about making and one question that needs another source. Keep the image and the separately excavated ship distinct.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the Met identifies a mid-tenth-century elephant-ivory panel, probably made in Constantinople and probably used privately. Missing side panels once completed a triptych. In a separate harbour excavation, the YK14 report records joining planks, sealing seams with caulking and repeated repairs. No cargo was recovered to connect that ship with this ivory. The openings are visible, probable private use is the museum’s interpretation, and transport on this ship is not established. Joining and sealing are two supported tasks; repairs show work after initial making, without supplying an exact repair date.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded urban/material-work reading, one source-qualified 843–1204 reference with a ninth–eleventh-century focus, three evidence readings and an answerable photograph/source-capsule activity. Complete original 330–1453 case interval, identity, claims, object order and earlier dimension texts retained; existing photograph bytes preserved. Selected renewals preserve prior dated source scopes. Modern image observations distinguish visible carving and letters from catalogue use and scholarly interpretation.
limitations: Met Description/Artwork Details/Public Domain and selected institutional essays were read, not complete provenance/inscription tabs, technical examination or linked books. Maker, patron, household, workshop, tusk source and transport route remain unknown; probable private use and probably Constantinople stay qualified.

YK14 consultation is limited to printed pp. 39–40 and 53–55 and exposed Table 2 on p. 47, not the entire paper, underlying dissertations, laboratory reports or actual figure pixels. Timber association, construction, pottery context, repairs and modern excavation are different clocks; no selected-icon cargo or exact sinking date established.

Frazer consultation covers selected text on pp. 153, 155–156 and 159–160, not the whole article, original Greek editions or figure pixels. Hades remains an attributed argument. The official Dumbarton Oaks household/monastic-document lead was inaccessible; no alternative mirror or original household document was read.

Existing photograph pixels were inspected unchanged. Photography date and current remote-image byte parity remain unverified. No new source plan or image reused or traced, numerical geographic locator accepted or missing triptych wings restored. The modern observation layer has its own date, credit and licence, separate from the ancient object and photograph. Small-screen and printed legibility require inspection of the final exports.
Independent historian/conservator/community review, real adult/family use, human screen-reader and physical-device/print acceptance remain open.
